reader_situation: A homeowner or renter whose breaker trips only when one particular pair runs at once (microwave plus toaster, space heater plus hair dryer, heater plus vacuum), while each appliance runs fine alone. They want to know whether it's a wiring problem, a bad breaker, or just too much on one circuit, and whether a fix is DIY.
direct_answer: Usually the two appliances are on the same circuit and their combined current is more than the breaker is rated for, so the breaker's heat-sensing element trips on the sustained overload. Read each nameplate wattage, divide by 120 volts to get amps, and add them: a 1,100 W microwave plus a 1,400 W toaster is about 20.8 A, more than a 15 A or 20 A breaker. Fix it by running them one at a time or on different circuits, never through an extension cord or power strip. If the breaker trips with one appliance alone, trips the instant you reset it, or comes with warm outlets or a burning smell, it's not a simple overload: call an electrician.
consensus: Two high-draw appliances on one circuit can exceed the breaker's rating and trip it.
Kitchen countertop appliances (microwave, toaster, kettle, coffee maker) and space heaters are common culprits.
Move one appliance to a different circuit or don't run them together.
Don't just install a bigger breaker.
If it keeps tripping, call an electrician.
gaps: Top results rarely show the arithmetic. Virginia Cooperative Extension says wattage is stamped on the nameplate, most US appliances use 120 volts, and you can multiply amps by volts; dividing nameplate watts by 120 gives amps a reader can add and compare with the number on the breaker handle.

Typical wattage ranges per appliance (VCE table) let a reader see which pairs overload a 15 A or a 20 A breaker even at the low end of the range (space heater plus hair dryer) and which only overload at the high end (microwave plus toaster).

Heat-sensing vs magnetic tripping explains the delay: Square D load-center breakers trip from heat generated by sustained low-level overload, but trip quickly when a magnetic coil senses a high-current short circuit. A trip after the pair has run a while points to overload; an instant trip points elsewhere.

Settings change the math: VCE notes actual power depends on the setting used, and one 1,500 W ceramic heater manual lists 700 W, 900 W and 1,500 W settings, so the low setting roughly halves its share of the circuit.

The appliance-vs-circuit test: UL Solutions says if an appliance trips the breaker no matter which outlet it's in, the appliance is the likely culprit; if one outlet repeatedly trips, the circuit is likely overloaded and needs a professional to upgrade it or add a line.

Extension cords and plug strips are not a fix: NFPA guidance (republished by Southwire) says they are not meant to carry the large loads of major appliances, and LG's microwave installation manual says not to use an extension cord.
Dimming lights when the second appliance starts are a sign the lights share the circuit with high-draw appliances (UL).

Manufacturer installation requirements: LG's over-the-range microwave manual says the outlet should be on a circuit dedicated to the microwave with a 15 or 20 A supply, so a microwave that shares with a toaster may not be installed as specified.

evidence.claim: Where to find wattage and how to get it from amps
evidence.detail: "Locate the wattage of most appliances stamped on the bottom or back of the appliance, or on its nameplate." If wattage isn't listed, measure current in amperes and multiply "by the voltage used by the appliance." "Most appliances in the United States use 120 volts."
evidence.source_title: Estimating Appliance and Home Electronic Energy Use (Virginia Cooperative Extension)

evidence.detail: Microwave oven 750–1100 W; toaster 800–1400 W; coffee maker 900–1200 W; hair dryer 1200–1875 W; heater (portable) 750–1500 W; vacuum cleaner 1000–1440 W; clothes iron 1000–1800 W; toaster oven 1225 W; refrigerator (frost-free, 16 cu ft) 725 W.
evidence.source_title: Estimating Appliance and Home Electronic Energy Use (Virginia Cooperative Extension)

evidence.detail: The wattage listed is the power drawn by the appliance, but the actual amount of power consumed depends on the setting used, because many appliances have multiple settings.
evidence.source_title: Estimating Appliance and Home Electronic Energy Use (Virginia Cooperative Extension)

evidence.claim: A 1,500 W heater's current and the manufacturer's circuit warning
evidence.detail: "This product is rated 12.5 amps (1500W) at 120V, 60 Hz." "This heater draws 12.5 amps in operation. To prevent overloading a circuit, do not plug the heater into a circuit that already has other appliances working." Heat settings: 1 ~ 700W, 2 ~ 900W, 3 ~ 1500W. Model NT15-20A, 1500W ceramic heater sold by Lowe's.

evidence.claim: One 1,500 W heater nearly fills a 15 A breaker
evidence.detail: If a 1,500-watt heater uses approximately 12.5 amps, a 15-amp breaker can handle only one such heater on the circuit, and very little else can be on when the heater is on. Read the instruction manual or check the data plate on the heater and do the calculations to prevent overloading the circuit.
evidence.source_title: Electrical space heaters (U.S. Army Combat Readiness/Safety Center)

evidence.detail: Square D load-center breakers "trip when heat is generated by sustained low-level overload current or quickly when the magnetic coil senses a high-current short circuit."
evidence.source_title: Square D Load-Center Circuit Breakers (McMaster-Carr catalog)

evidence.detail: Breakers and fuses are designed to trip to prevent overloads. If a vacuum or hair dryer trips the breaker no matter which outlet it's plugged into, the appliance is the likely culprit. If one outlet repeatedly blows the same fuse, the circuit is likely overloaded and needs a professional to upgrade it or add a line.
evidence.source_title: 8 Signs You May Have a Problem with Your Electrical Wiring (UL Solutions)

evidence.claim: Dimming lights point to high-draw appliances on the same circuit
evidence.detail: Because light fixtures typically draw only a small amount of power, flickering or dimming usually comes from high-draw appliances or space heaters on the same circuit; an electrician can move the lights to another circuit or add dedicated lines.
evidence.source_title: 8 Signs You May Have a Problem with Your Electrical Wiring (UL Solutions)

evidence.detail: A switch plate may be slightly warm, but the outlet that powers it should never become hot. If an outlet is uncomfortably hot, turn off the device and try another outlet; if it gets hot with nothing plugged in, it may be wired incorrectly, so consult an electrician.
evidence.source_title: 8 Signs You May Have a Problem with Your Electrical Wiring (UL Solutions)

evidence.claim: GFCIs are a separate shock-protection device
evidence.detail: Kitchens and bathrooms need "special shock-resistant outlets called ground fault circuit interrupters (GFCIs)."
evidence.source_title: 8 Signs You May Have a Problem with Your Electrical Wiring (UL Solutions)

evidence.detail: Call a qualified electrician or your landlord if you have: frequent problems with blowing fuses or tripping circuit breakers; a tingling feeling when you touch an electrical appliance; discolored or warm wall outlets; a burning or rubbery smell coming from an appliance; flickering or dimming lights; sparks from an outlet.
evidence.source_title: Electrical Safety tip sheet (NFPA, distributed by the Kentucky State Fire Marshal)

evidence.claim: One heat-producing appliance per outlet; no cords or strips for big loads
evidence.detail: Tips from the NFPA: "Only plug one heat-producing appliance into a receptacle outlet at a time" (coffee makers, toasters, space heaters). "Extension cords and plug strips should not be used because they are not meant to carry the large loads" of major appliances. "Extension cords are intended for temporary use"; have a qualified electrician add receptacle outlets.
evidence.source_title: Top 9 Electrical Safety Tips to Help Prevent Electrical Fires (Southwire)

evidence.claim: Microwave installation calls for a dedicated circuit
evidence.detail: "The outlet should be on a circuit dedicated to the microwave oven (120V, 60 Hz., AC only) with a 15 or 20A fused electrical supply." If you do not have the proper wall outlet, you must have one installed by a qualified electrician. "Do not use an extension cord."

real_questions: Why does my breaker trip when the microwave and toaster (or kettle) run at the same time but not separately?
Why does it take a minute or two to trip instead of tripping right away?
Can I just put in a 20 amp breaker?
Which outlets are on the same circuit?
Space heater and hair dryer in the bathroom keep tripping the breaker: is that dangerous?

original_asset.spec: Pair-load table: common pairs with VCE wattage ranges summed at low and high end, converted to amps at 120 V (amps = watts ÷ 120), compared with 15 A and 20 A breaker ratings. Microwave+toaster 1,550–2,500 W = 12.9–20.8 A; microwave+coffee maker 1,650–2,300 W = 13.8–19.2 A; toaster oven+coffee maker 2,125–2,425 W = 17.7–20.2 A; heater+vacuum 1,750–2,940 W = 14.6–24.5 A; heater+hair dryer 1,950–3,375 W = 16.3–28.1 A. Worked example: heater manual's 700 W setting + 1,100 W microwave = 1,800 W = 15.0 A vs 1,500 W + 1,100 W = 2,600 W = 21.7 A.

cautions: Don't upsize the breaker; UL says an overloaded circuit needs a professional to upgrade it or add a line.
No extension cords or power strips for heaters, microwaves or other heat-producing appliances.
Instant trips, trips with one appliance, warm/discolored outlets, burning smell, tingling or sparks: stop and call an electrician (NFPA).
Breaker trip timing isn't a published number in these sources; describe it qualitatively.
Don't present 'amps = watts ÷ 120' as an exact measurement; nameplate wattage is the listed draw, and settings change it.
